speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the outset, Sir, let me say this: no woman or man should have to suffer the indignity of her or his modesty being insulted or outraged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a society, we must make sure these values are maintained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People must feel safe, as they go about their life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our laws must and enforcement must underpin these values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The questions by Members relate to: (a) the statistics relating to sexual offences in our universities; (b) the way in which the Police and the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) exercise their discretion in deciding to prosecute or not prosecute an offender, and the general approach taken by Police and AGC on cases relating to sexual misconduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah have asked about the cases of sexual misconduct in the AUs that were reported to the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supervised probation was imposed by the Courts in four cases and a discharge not amounting to an acquittal was given by the Court in one case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the sentencing for one case where the offender has been convicted is still pending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that leaves a remainder of 15, out of the total of 31 cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 13 of these cases, a conditional warning was given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourteen of the 15 students who were administered warnings, or 93%, did not re-offend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The one National University of Singapore (NUS) student who re-offended had originally been issued with a conditional warning for a voyeurism offence he committed in 2015.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, beyond these 56 cases, there were an additional eight cases reported directly to the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of these eight, there was insufficient evidence in six cases, and investigations in another two cases are ongoing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police had earlier also clarified some factual inaccuracies in media reporting of cases for AY2015/2016 and AY2017/2018.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were 25 cases of sexual offences brought before the NUS Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of these 25, 17 were reported to the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nine of the 17 were prosecuted in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts handed down imprisonment terms in five of those cases; they gave supervised probation for three cases and gave discharge not amounting to an acquittal in one case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In another seven of the 17 reported cases, the Police administered conditional warnings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the media articles had also erroneously published that there were 13 repeat offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on Police records, there was only one repeat offender, and I had referred to that case earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These numbers show that some have been prosecuted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Depending on the facts, others have been given a second chance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are no "free passes" to university students or anyone else.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had, some time ago, asked the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to review sexual offences, in particular, offences against: (a)	children – people will remember the Joshua Robinson case; and (b) women – outraging modesty, insulting modesty and other offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I had also given directions to toughen our laws in these areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Following the review by the Penal Code Review Committee as well as my Ministry, we decided that some new offences should be specified in law and sentences for some existing offences should be enhanced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Voyeurism is now dealt with under "Insulting the Modesty of a Woman" in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The proposal is to make it a standalone offence and increase the penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also proposed the updating of some existing offences to deal with technological developments which enable predatory behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is all set out in the Penal Code (Amendment) Bill, tabled in Parliament in February.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Parliament passes the Bill into law, then voyeurism, usually known as "Peeping Tom" behaviour, as well as the making, possessing, accessing and distributing of voyeuristic materials, will all be criminalised as specific offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be presumed that the victims in such recordings did not consent to being recorded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That deals with the evidential challenge sometimes of identifying victims in such recordings, and the penalties will be enhanced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because of Parliamentary rules, I should not go into any further detail on the proposed changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will be debating it and, of course, these changes were conceptualised, put through, drafted and tabled in Parliament before the latest discussions on these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The proposals show the Government’s underlying approach and philosophy towards sexual offences where the victims are, of course, predominantly women.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We take it very seriously, we want to send a very strong signal that would deter would-be offenders and protect victims, who, as I said, are predominantly women.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Penal Code changes have been thought through for over a year now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of this – being tough, taking a no-nonsense approach – does not mean that every offender must be or will be automatically charged in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police and AGC must look at the facts of each case and exercise discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was an NUS student, he had taken videos of children in a toilet in a shopping mall, which happened over two days in 2015.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After he was charged, the Police and AGC received a medical report from his doctor at the Institute of Mental Health (IMH).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The assessment was that his risk of re-offending was low and he would benefit from continual mental health treatment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he was put in jail, that could get affected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact that he did not have any prior history was also relevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has since completed the 24-month warning period; no further re-offending, and he has remained crime-free.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The data I have shown indicates in several other cases prosecutions were carried out for offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, we are going to make them even tougher if Parliament agrees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are creating new laws as well but we must also enforce them appropriately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When a woman’s privacy has been violated, the follow-up actions must ensure that she is treated with dignity and respect, and her concerns must be addressed and she must be supported.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The criminal legal framework must deal with the offender in a way that ensures the specific victim’s safety, deal with the specific offender and deter other would-be offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this respect, when such violation takes place in, say, NUS, there are actions that NUS has to take and there are actions that the Police have to take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police will investigate, decide on the best course of action after investigations, whether to prosecute, not prosecute, and what is the right thing to do on all the factors, ensure that their decision will protect the victim and uphold deterrence and safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our laws and the way we enforce our laws have ensured that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These figures have been consistently high over the years, and we want to make sure that that continues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can be assured that the Government is committed to continue keeping the environment safe and being tough on such offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why, as I said earlier, we have reviewed the Penal Code provisions, and are proposing new offences and seeking to enhance penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Broadly, the approach is to consider the specific facts and circumstances of the case, the severity of the offence, including the evidence, and aggravating or mitigating factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police will also consider how other similar cases had been treated to ensure consistency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the interest of fairness, like cases should be treated like other like cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Attorney-General, as the Public Prosecutor, makes the final decision based on his prosecutorial discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Specific facts, and I say this by way of illustration, could include previous criminal record, if any; level of remorse, whether the offender comes clean, cooperates; and whether any videos of the victim have been posted online or otherwise shared.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police also assess the likelihood of rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police make such assessments regularly, when making decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will then recommend the course of action: to prosecute, or give a conditional warning, or a stern warning, or to take no further action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should add that in these cases, the assessment of future conduct and possible rehabilitation is quite important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is so even when the offender had done similar acts previously, which will, of course, weigh against him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police will look at all the factors, including the level of remorse, whether he owned up voluntarily, the likelihood of reform and the likelihood of re-offending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will also, of course, consider the circumstances of the victim, the impact of the offence on the victim and the need for deterrence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Generally, there would be no reason for the Police to show any leniency, if the following aggravating factors are present: (a)	a person has previous convictions or was warned for similar offences; (b)	premeditation and deception in committing the offence, for example, by using hidden pinhole cameras, masking his face, covering closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras, or other means to evade detection; (c)	the video had been shared or circulated; or (d)	the perpetrator was not remorseful or had been uncooperative in the investigation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A 23-year-old man filmed a woman showering at Republic Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The accused had committed the offences over a period of four months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He tried to evade detection by covering his face with a towel, covering up CCTVs in the vicinity and did not own up voluntarily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The man was charged and sentenced to 10 weeks’ imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A conditional warning means that (a) an offender has been put on notice; (b) he would know that the authorities have enough evidence and are prepared to press charges against him if he does not reform; (c) if he commits a fresh offence during this period, he would be liable to be prosecuted for both the current offence and the subsequent fresh or new offence; in other words, he is not let off the hook for the earlier offence; he will pay for both.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have not specifically asked about Mr Nicholas Lim’s case, involving Ms Monica Baey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The factors that were taken into account in his case were set out in the Police statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is, therefore, best that I do not go into it in detail on the factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But briefly, there were factors which could have justified charging him, the primary one, of course, being that he had done something very wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These factors were weighed against other factors, which would justify giving him another chance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police weighed both sets of factors and decided that a conditional warning was appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was one of those cases, quite usual, normal for the Police, where the decision was based on judgement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police assessed him to be remorseful and likely to reform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He confessed voluntarily within minutes of the offence being committed and well before any Police report was made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other factors have also been mentioned in the Police statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A conditional warning has been an effective deterrent for offenders who have had good propensity to reform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even after the stipulated crime-free period, the warning remains an internal record for calibrating future prosecutorial decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perpetrators who receive warnings are told in clear terms that if they re-offend, they will face serious consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the cases at the AUs show, most who were given conditional warnings did not re-offend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Several perpetrators have been prosecuted and put behind bars.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the rigid meting out of uniform penalties will not serve the wider public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked about victim care and public education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One area which we continuously review is how to further improve on the support given to victims of sexual crimes who experienced emotional, psychological damage and stress.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the years, we have made significant improvements to Police processes and the way Police officers interact with victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have a response framework to ensure that victims of sexual crimes are attended to quickly and a victim care programme that provides emotional support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will be given concerted publicity, to raise awareness about the new sexual offences, including voyeurism, when it is classified as a standalone offence, and the enhanced penalties.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, who is the qualified person to make the assessment on the accused's suitability for rehabilitation?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is this process applied to all accused persons?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many felt that MHA gave more consideration to the offender than the traumatised victim as the future of perpetrators was mentioned.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But what about the potential long-term or even possible permanent damage to the victim?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can MHA ensure that victims are given fair consideration, if not more?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The third supplementary question: it is not just about Monica Baey and Nicholas Lim.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to send a strong signal to everyone that we have zero tolerance for sexual harassment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with the Minister that we need tougher laws, but I disagree that, in sentencing, we compare like-for-like.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the sentencing should be heavier, compared to the previous one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I hope, the Minister will consider that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Who makes the decision on assessment for rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I went into the factors in some detail just now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not just for victims of sexual offences, but other offences, too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But of course, within the framework of the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why you take into account the severity of the offence, the impact on the victim, the need to deter others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within that, you also look at the offender and you make an assessment based on how cooperative he has been.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are sitting down, you are talking to him, you see whether he confessed or he tried to hide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean that the assessments will be perfect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not often that MHA or the Singapore Government is being accused of being soft on these sorts of issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Usually, the complaints are the reverse, that not enough mercy is shown.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we err on the side of being tough.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, you look at the facts of each case and, where it is possible to exercise discretion, you do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is done by the Police as well as by AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point is that MHA gives consideration to the offenders, when, really, more concern and care should be given to the victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not just for the victim but also to deter similar conduct and it will protect others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason why the crime rate in Singapore is so low is because people generally understand a few things: one, if you commit an offence, it is likely that you will be caught; second, if you are caught, there is a very high likelihood that you will be charged, depending on the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are charged, there is a very high likelihood that you will be found guilty because the investigation will be thorough, the facts will be presented, there is a professional set of lawyers dealing with it and the Courts are staffed by highly trained lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if the evidence is presented, properly assessed, then it is likely to result in a conviction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, of course, if there is no evidence, or the evidence is weak, it will be thrown out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, AGC would often not even proceed on the basis of there being no adequate evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this framework is well understood on the ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is one of the reasons why the crime rate is low as well in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot do something and get away with it, by and large.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How is it balanced, what were the factors that are taken into account, I have said in specific cases in my answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I agree that as a method of approach and principle, yes, of course, what has happened to the victim is extremely important and nothing I say detracts from that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, we have to send a strong signal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I meant by "like-for-like" was this: you have a set of facts, a certain decision was taken to prosecute or to give a conditional warning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Consistency does not mean leniency, please do not mistake me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Consistency means you have decided to charge, then you will decide in a subsequent case to charge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you have decided to give conditional warning and the factors are broadly similar, then you will tend towards giving a conditional warning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, of course, you will look at whether there are any other factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is more that there has got to be a certain consistency in the way the law is applied and processed, not just in the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, we can look at the precedence for consistency, but also from the perspective of the Police and AGC.
